subject: mathematics
question_text: By using Cramer's rule, solve 2x − y + 3z = 9, x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2.

mark_split.label: Write the system as AX = D
Find Δ = det A and check it is not zero
Apply Cramer's rule and state the solution

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.27 — LAQ chapter 3 Matrices, answer 18.1, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page). Printed appearances: AP 16 · TS 17. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S. Book p.27 sets two Cramer questions side by side in two columns, which leaves no margin for the [N Marks] tags the chapter uses elsewhere, so no split is printed for any of the four Cramer answers. The 1+1+1+1+1+2 above follows the only split this book states for a solving-a-system question — the note on book p.30 reading 'Just finding A⁻¹ gives u 4 Marks. For remaining steps u get 3 Marks', which weights the bulk computation against the finish. Here that bulk is four determinants, so each carries one mark and the rule plus the answer carry two. A teacher may weight Δ higher, since a zero Δ would make Cramer's rule inapplicable. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all four Cramer answers in this unit, deliberately: the four questions are one method over different numbers. Star rank is the CHAPTER's ★★★, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to the "Apply Cramer's rule and state the solution" step.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by Cramer's rule — say what four determinants you need, how you build each one, and how you get x, y and z at the end.

steps.label: Write it as AX = D
steps.margin_note: First mark. A holds the coefficients in the order they appear, X holds the unknowns, D holds the right-hand sides. Write the equations out in x, y, z order before building A — a missing term is the commonest error in the whole question.
steps.memory_tip: Line the equations up in x, y, z order first, so A holds the coefficients in the right places.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That the system is written as AX = D, with A the coefficient matrix, X the column of unknowns and D the column of constants.
accept: write the system as A X equals D where A is the coefficient matrix X is x y z and D is the constants
put it in matrix form with the coefficients in A the unknowns in X and the right hand sides in D
first write A X equals D taking the coefficients into A
modata AX equals D form lo rasta, A lo coefficients, D lo right side values
form the coefficient matrix the variable column and the constant column

steps.why: Cramer's rule is a fixed procedure applied to this matrix. Getting A right is the only place where the original equations are used, so every later step inherits any mistake made here.
common_mistakes: Writing the coefficients in the order they appear rather than in x, y, z order.
Missing a coefficient of 1 or −1 because the letter is written with no number in front.
Putting the constants into A instead of D.

steps.label: Find Δ
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Δ is the determinant of A itself. It has to be non-zero or Cramer's rule cannot be used at all — so say so in writing, do not just compute the number.
steps.memory_tip: Δ is the determinant of A itself, and it must be NON-ZERO or the rule cannot be used. Say so in writing.

recall.must_convey: That Δ is the determinant of the coefficient matrix, that it works out to −2, and that being non-zero is what allows Cramer's rule to be used.
accept: delta is the determinant of A which comes to minus two and since it is not zero cramer's rule can be used
find the determinant of the coefficient matrix it is minus two not equal to zero
expand det A to get minus two which is non zero so the method works
delta equals det A minus two, zero kaadu kabatti cramer rule use cheyyochu
the determinant of A is minus two and it must be non zero for this rule

steps.why: Cramer's rule divides by Δ. If Δ were zero the division would be impossible and the system would have either no solution or infinitely many — so the check is part of the method, not a formality.
common_mistakes: Computing Δ but never writing that it is non-zero.
Getting the sign pattern wrong when expanding: it is plus, minus, plus along the top row.
Using the constants column somewhere inside Δ.

steps.label: Find Δ₁
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Δ₁ is Δ with the FIRST column replaced by the constants 9, 6, 2. Columns 2 and 3 are untouched. Replace, never insert.
steps.memory_tip: Δ₁ REPLACES the first column with the constants. Columns 2 and 3 are untouched — replace, never insert.
lines: Replace C₁ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₁ is formed by replacing the first column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to −2.
accept: delta one is delta with the first column replaced by nine six two and it comes to minus two
put the constants into the first column and expand to get minus two
replace column one with the right hand side values giving delta one equal to minus two
first column place lo constants pettithe delta one minus two vasthundi
swap the first column for the constant column and the determinant is minus two

steps.why: Δ₁ pairs with x because x is the first unknown. The subscript is a position, not a name — which is why the constants go into column one and nowhere else.
common_mistakes: Replacing a row instead of a column.
Replacing the second column and later dividing it into x.
Adding a fourth column instead of replacing one.

steps.label: Find Δ₂
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Same move, second column. Column 1 goes back to the coefficients of x — a common slip is to leave the constants there from the previous step.
steps.memory_tip: Second column now, and column 1 goes BACK to the x coefficients. Leaving the constants there is the usual slip.
lines: Replace C₂ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₂ is formed by replacing the second column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to −4.
accept: delta two is delta with the second column replaced by the constants and it equals minus four
put nine six two into the middle column and expand to get minus four
replace column two with the constant column giving minus four
second column lo constants pettithe delta two minus four vasthundi
the middle column becomes the constants and the determinant is minus four

steps.why: Each unknown gets the determinant whose replaced column is that unknown's own column in A. y sits in column two, so Δ₂ is y's determinant.
common_mistakes: Leaving the constants in column one from the previous step, so two columns are wrong at once.
Forgetting the minus in front of the middle term when expanding along the top row.

steps.label: Find Δ₃
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Last one — third column replaced, the other two back to the coefficients.
steps.memory_tip: Third column replaced, the other two back to the coefficients.
lines: Replace C₃ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₃ is formed by replacing the third column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to −6.
accept: delta three is delta with the third column replaced by the constants and it comes to minus six
put the constants into the last column and expand to get minus six
replace column three with nine six two giving minus six
third column lo constants pettithe delta three minus six vasthundi
the last column becomes the constants and the determinant is minus six

steps.why: Three unknowns need three replaced determinants, plus Δ itself. Four determinants is always the cost of Cramer's rule on a 3×3 system, and knowing that in advance is how you budget the time.
common_mistakes: Stopping after Δ₂ and trying to find z by substitution.
Leaving an earlier replacement in place.

steps.label: Apply Cramer's rule
steps.margin_note: The last three marks. Each unknown is its own determinant divided by Δ. All four values here are negative, so every division gives a positive answer — write the divisions out rather than doing them in your head.
steps.memory_tip: Each unknown is its own determinant over Δ. All four values are negative here, so every answer comes out positive.

recall.must_convey: That each unknown is its own determinant divided by Δ, giving x = 1, y = 2, z = 3. The division rule must be stated, not just the answers.
accept: x is delta one by delta y is delta two by delta and z is delta three by delta giving one two and three
divide each of the three determinants by delta to get x equals one y equals two z equals three
by cramer's rule each unknown is its own determinant over delta so the solution is one two three
prathi determinant ni delta tho divide cheste x one y two z three vasthundi
delta one over delta gives x equals one and similarly y is two and z is three
reject: x is one y is two z is three

steps.why: The whole method exists so that each unknown can be found on its own, without eliminating anything. That is also why an error in one determinant spoils only one unknown.
common_mistakes: Dividing Δ by Δ₁ instead of Δ₁ by Δ.
Losing a sign: a negative divided by a negative is positive.
Never substituting back to check — putting x=1, y=2, z=3 into the first equation gives 2−2+9 = 9.

insider_note: Four determinants are needed, and Δ must come first — if it were 0, Cramer's rule would not apply at all. Every Δ here is negative, so all three divisions give positive answers.
